questions.stem: Data that is normally distributed is represented by a curve that is:
options: flat, with all values equally common
bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean
bell-shaped with a long tail to the right
U-shaped with peaks at both extremes
questions.explanation: The normal curve is a symmetric bell shape, highest at the mean and tailing off equally on both sides. A long tail to one side describes skewed data.

questions.stem: For data that is normally distributed, the mean, median and mode are:
options: in the order median < mean < mode
approximately equal
in the order mean < median < mode
in the order mode < median < mean
questions.explanation: Because the normal distribution is symmetric with a single peak, its centre is the mean, the median and the mode all at once. In skewed data they separate.

questions.stem: Which dataset is most likely to be approximately normally distributed?
options: The weekly incomes of all Australian workers
The numbers rolled on a fair die many times
The ages of people at a primary school
The heights of adult women in Australia
questions.explanation: Heights of a large adult population cluster symmetrically around the mean. Incomes are skewed by a few very high earners, die rolls are uniform, and school ages are bunched among children.

questions.stem: Two normal distributions have the same mean, but distribution P has a larger standard deviation than distribution Q. Compared with Q's curve, P's curve is:
options: wider and flatter, centred at the same place
narrower and taller, centred at the same place
the same shape, moved to the right
the same shape, moved to the left
questions.explanation: A larger standard deviation spreads the data further from the mean, so the curve is wider and, with the same total area, lower. Changing the mean, not the standard deviation, moves the curve sideways.

questions.stem: A z-score tells you:
options: the difference between a value and the mean, in the data's units
how many values in the dataset are greater than the mean
how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean
the percentage of the data that lies below a particular value
questions.explanation: z = (x − μ)/σ measures distance from the mean in standard deviations. The difference x − μ alone is in the data's units; dividing by σ makes it a z-score.

questions.stem: The z-scores of a normally distributed dataset have:
options: a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1
a mean of 1 and a standard deviation of 0
a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0
the same mean and standard deviation as the data
questions.explanation: Subtracting the mean shifts the centre to 0, and dividing by the standard deviation scales the spread to 1. This is why z-scores from different datasets can be compared.

questions.stem: In the formula z = (x − μ)/σ, the symbol σ stands for:
options: the mean of the data
the number of data values
the standard deviation of the data
the sum of all the data values
questions.explanation: σ (sigma) is the standard deviation and μ (mu) is the mean. Dividing by σ expresses the distance from the mean in standard deviations.

questions.stem: A value has a z-score of 0. This means the value is:
options: equal to zero
the smallest value
one standard deviation below the mean
equal to the mean
questions.explanation: z = 0 means x − μ = 0, so the value is exactly at the mean, whatever the units of the data.

questions.stem: Test marks have a mean of 65 and a standard deviation of 5. What is the z-score of a mark of 78?
questions.explanation: z = (78 − 65) ÷ 5 = 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6. 13 is the difference from the mean in marks, before dividing by the standard deviation.

questions.stem: Times have a mean of 60 seconds and a standard deviation of 4 seconds. What is the z-score of a time of 52 seconds?
questions.explanation: z = (52 − 60) ÷ 4 = −8 ÷ 4 = −2. The value is below the mean, so its z-score is negative. −0.5 divides 4 by −8 instead of −8 by 4.

questions.stem: Heights have a mean of 170 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm. Which height has a z-score of −1.5?
options: 182 cm
162 cm
158 cm
questions.explanation: Rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ: x = μ + zσ = 170 + (−1.5)(8) = 170 − 12 = 158 cm. 182 cm uses +1.5, and 168.5 cm subtracts 1.5 cm instead of 1.5 standard deviations.

questions.stem: Sam scored 72 in Maths (mean 60, standard deviation 8) and 75 in English (mean 70, standard deviation 4). In which subject did Sam do better relative to the class?
options: English, with z = 1.25 compared with 1.5
English, because 75 is higher than 72
Both equally, because both are above the mean
Maths, with z = 1.5 compared with 1.25
questions.explanation: Maths: z = (72 − 60) ÷ 8 = 1.5. English: z = (75 − 70) ÷ 4 = 1.25. Sam is further above the class mean in Maths. Comparing raw marks ignores the different means and spreads.

questions.stem: Mia scored 58 in Science (mean 64, standard deviation 4) and 61 in History (mean 70, standard deviation 9). In which subject did she perform better relative to the class?
options: Science, because 6 marks below is less than 9
History, with z = −1 compared with −1.5
Science, with z = −1.5 compared with −1
History, because 61 is higher than 58
questions.explanation: Science: z = (58 − 64) ÷ 4 = −1.5. History: z = (61 − 70) ÷ 9 = −1. Both are below the mean, but −1 is closer to it, so History was the better relative result. Mia was further below the mean in marks in History, but its spread is larger.

questions.stem: Student A has a z-score of 1.2 in a test where the class mean was 55. Student B, in a different class, has a z-score of 0.8 where the class mean was 70. Which statement is correct?
options: B performed better relative to their class, as 70 is higher than 55
The two results cannot be compared, because the means are different
B performed better relative to their class, as 0.8 is closer to 1
A performed better relative to their class than B did
questions.explanation: z-scores remove the effect of different means and spreads, so they can be compared directly. A higher z-score means a better relative performance, so A did better.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule: about 68% of values have z-scores between −1 and 1, about 95% between −2 and 2, and about 99.7% between −3 and 3.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values have z-scores between −2 and 2?
questions.explanation: About 95% of values lie within two standard deviations of the mean. 47.5% is only the half between 0 and 2.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values lie more than three standard deviations from the mean?
questions.explanation: About 99.7% lie within three standard deviations, so about 100% − 99.7% = 0.3% lie outside, split equally between the two tails (0.15% in each).

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values have a z-score greater than 1?
questions.explanation: 68% lie between z = −1 and 1, leaving 32% outside, split equally between the two tails: 16% above z = 1. 84% is the percentage below z = 1.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values have a z-score less than −2?
questions.explanation: 95% lie between z = −2 and 2, so 5% lie outside, half in each tail: 2.5% below z = −2. 5% counts both tails.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values have z-scores between −1 and 2?
questions.explanation: From −1 to 0 is half of 68%, 34%; from 0 to 2 is half of 95%, 47.5%. Total 34% + 47.5% = 81.5%.

questions.stem: For a normally distributed dataset, what is the probability that a randomly chosen score has a z-score between 2 and 3?
questions.explanation: Between 0 and 3 is 99.7% ÷ 2 = 49.85%, and between 0 and 2 is 95% ÷ 2 = 47.5%. So between 2 and 3 is 2.35%, a probability of 0.0235. 0.047 counts both tails.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values lie between the mean and one standard deviation above it?
questions.explanation: By symmetry, the 68% within one standard deviation is split equally on each side of the mean, so 34% lie between the mean and z = 1.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values are below the mean?
questions.explanation: The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so half of the values, 50%, are below it.

questions.stem: Heights of adult men are normally distributed with mean 175 cm and standard deviation 6 cm. Approximately what percentage are between 169 cm and 187 cm?
Lengths of fish are normally distributed with mean 50 cm and standard deviation 5 cm. Approximately what percentage of the fish are between 40 cm and 60 cm long?
questions.explanation: 40 cm and 60 cm are each 10 cm, or two standard deviations, from the mean, so z runs from −2 to 2 and about 95% of the fish lie between them. 68% would be for 45 cm to 55 cm.

questions.stem: Heights are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 6 cm. Approximately what percentage of heights are between 152 cm and 176 cm?
questions.explanation: 152 cm has z = −3 and 176 cm has z = 1. From −3 to 0 is 99.7% ÷ 2 = 49.85%, and from 0 to 1 is 34%, giving 83.85%. 81.5% uses 47.5% (the z = −2 value) instead of 49.85%.

questions.stem: 800 students sat a test whose marks were normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 10. Approximately how many students scored above 90?
questions.explanation: 90 has z = (90 − 70) ÷ 10 = 2, and about 2.5% score above z = 2. 2.5% of 800 = 20. 40 uses 5%, which counts both tails.

questions.stem: Battery lifetimes are normally distributed with mean 400 hours and standard deviation 25 hours. In a batch of 2000 batteries, about how many would last less than 350 hours?
questions.explanation: 350 hours has z = (350 − 400) ÷ 25 = −2, and about 2.5% lie below z = −2. 2.5% of 2000 = 50. 320 uses 16%, the tail below z = −1.

questions.stem: The mass of cereal in a box is normally distributed with mean 500 g and standard deviation 4 g. What is the probability that a randomly chosen box contains more than 508 g?
questions.explanation: 508 g has z = (508 − 500) ÷ 4 = 2. About 2.5% of values lie above z = 2, a probability of 0.025. 0.475 is the probability of being between the mean and z = 2.

questions.stem: On a normal curve, the probability that a score has a z-score greater than 1 is represented by:
options: the area under the curve between z = 0 and 1
the area under the curve to the right of z = 1
the area under the curve to the left of z = 1
the height of the curve at the point z = 1
questions.explanation: Probabilities are areas under the curve, with the total area equal to 1. 'Greater than 1' is the area to the right of z = 1, about 16% of the total.

questions.stem: About 95% of a normally distributed dataset lies between 40 and 80. What are the mean and standard deviation?
options: Mean 40, standard deviation 20
Mean 60, standard deviation 10
Mean 60, standard deviation 20
Mean 60, standard deviation 40
questions.explanation: 95% lies within two standard deviations either side of the mean, so the mean is the midpoint, 60, and 80 − 60 = 20 is two standard deviations: σ = 10. σ = 20 forgets that the interval spans two standard deviations each side.

questions.stem: About 68% of a normally distributed dataset lies between 45 and 55. What is the standard deviation?
questions.explanation: 68% lies within one standard deviation of the mean, so the mean is 50 and one standard deviation is 55 − 50 = 5. 10 is the width of the whole interval.

questions.stem: A machine fills bottles with a mean of 500 mL and a standard deviation of 4 mL, normally distributed. A bottle is found with 486 mL. What is the best judgement?
options: Its z-score is −3.5, which is very unusual, so the machine should be checked
Its z-score is −14, which is impossible, so the measurement must be wrong
Its z-score is −3.5, but about 16% of bottles are this low, so it is normal
Its z-score is −1.4, which is within the normal range, so no action is needed
questions.explanation: z = (486 − 500) ÷ 4 = −3.5. Fewer than 0.15% of values lie below z = −3, so a bottle this low is very rare and suggests a fault. −14 is the difference in mL, not the z-score.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, what is the probability that a randomly chosen score is less extreme than a z-score of 2, that is, between −2 and 2?
questions.explanation: Less extreme than ±2 means within two standard deviations of the mean, about 95% of values, so the probability is 0.95. 0.975 is the probability of being below z = 2.

questions.stem: For normally distributed data, approximately what percentage of values have a z-score less than 1?
questions.explanation: Below the mean is 50%, and from z = 0 to z = 1 is 34%, so 50% + 34% = 84% lie below z = 1. 16% is the percentage above z = 1.

questions.stem: A company says its light globes last 1000 hours on average, with a standard deviation of 50 hours, normally distributed. It replaces any globe that fails before 900 hours. About what percentage of globes will it replace?
questions.explanation: 900 hours has z = (900 − 1000) ÷ 50 = −2, and about 2.5% of values lie below z = −2. 5% counts both tails, including globes lasting more than 1100 hours, which are not replaced.
